module: C1 Atomic Structure and Periodic Table

Atomic Structure.intro: The atom is the basic unit of all matter. Understanding atomic structure is essential for all of chemistry.
Atomic Structure.mnemonic: Pretty Neat Electrons: Protons (positive) and Neutrons (neutral) in the Nucleus; Electrons on the outside. Or remember: 'Protons Plus Neutrons = Mass number, Protons Only = Atomic number' — PPNM, PO!

sections.title: Structure of the Atom
sections.text: The atom has a tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons arranged in shells. The atom is almost entirely empty space.
points: Nucleus — contains protons (charge +1) and neutrons (charge 0); extremely small and dense
Electrons — charge −1; orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels); negligible mass
Proton number (atomic number) — the number of protons in the nucleus; identifies the element
Mass number — total number of protons + neutrons in the nucleus
Neutrons — mass number − atomic number = number of neutrons
Neutral atom — number of protons always equals number of electrons; overall charge is zero

sections.title: Isotopes
sections.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, giving them different mass numbers.
points: Same element — same atomic number (proton number), so same chemical properties
Different mass — different number of neutrons, so different mass number and physical properties
Carbon-12 vs Carbon-14 — both have 6 protons; C-12 has 6 neutrons, C-14 has 8 neutrons
Hydrogen isotopes — hydrogen (1p, 0n), deuterium (1p, 1n), tritium (1p, 2n)
Radioactive isotopes — some isotopes are unstable and emit radiation (e.g. C-14 used in carbon dating)
Worked example — Chlorine has two isotopes: Cl-35 (75%) and Cl-37 (25%), giving Ar ≈ 35.5

sections.title: Relative Atomic Mass and Electronic Configuration
sections.text: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average mass of an element's isotopes. Electronic configuration describes how electrons fill shells around the nucleus.
points: Relative atomic mass (Ar) — weighted average of all isotope masses, accounting for their abundance
Formula — Ar = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) ÷ 100
Shell 1 — holds max 2 electrons; Shells 2 and 3 — hold max 8 electrons each
Electronic configuration of sodium — 11 electrons arranged as 2, 8, 1
Outer shell electrons — determine chemical properties and group number in the periodic table

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Relative atomic mass (Ar) = weighted average mass of all isotopes, taking into account their relative abundance.

keyTerms.def: Number of protons in the nucleus — defines the element
Total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Weighted average mass of an element's isotopes, accounting for abundance
An energy level around the nucleus where electrons are found
The arrangement of electrons in shells around an atom's nucleus (e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium)
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons

examTips: Atomic number = number of protons = number of electrons (in a neutral atom) — state all three in exam answers.
Mass number − atomic number = number of neutrons; this is the calculation AQA most commonly asks.
Isotopes have the SAME atomic number (same element) but DIFFERENT mass numbers (different neutron count).
When calculating relative atomic mass, show the formula and working: Ar = (mass₁ × abundance₁ + mass₂ × abundance₂) ÷ 100.
commonMistakes: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons — they do NOT. Only the neutron number differs; proton number is identical.
Confusing mass number (protons + neutrons) with atomic number (protons only) — mass number is always larger or equal.
Forgetting that electrons have negligible mass — only protons and neutrons contribute to mass number.
clozePassages: An atom consists of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. Protons have a positive charge, neutrons have no charge, and electrons have a negative charge. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom, so the overall charge is zero. The atomic number is the number of protons and identifies the element.

The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon atoms but carbon-14 has two extra neutrons. The relative atomic mass takes into account the abundance of each isotope.

Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, the second and third shells hold up to 8 electrons each. The arrangement of electrons is called the electronic configuration. The number of electrons in the outer shell determines the chemical properties of the element. Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of outer shell electrons.

Ions are atoms or groups of atoms that have gained or lost electrons and have an overall electric charge. A cation is a positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons. An anion is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons. The charge of an ion depends on how many electrons are gained or lost. Metal atoms tend to form cations; non-metal atoms tend to form anions.

The Periodic Table.intro: The periodic table organises all known elements by their atomic structure. Understanding its layout is fundamental to chemistry.
The Periodic Table.mnemonic: Remember periods and groups with 'Periods go across the Page; Groups Go down like a Gangway' — P across, G down. For electron shells: 'Period 1 = 1 shell, Period 2 = 2 shells' and so on.

sections.title: Organisation of the Periodic Table
sections.text: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. The position of an element reveals its electronic structure and chemical behaviour.
points: Atomic number order — elements arranged left to right, top to bottom by increasing proton number
Periods (rows) — elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells
Groups (columns) — elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons → similar properties
Group number — equals the number of outer shell electrons for groups 1–7 (e.g. Group 2 = 2 outer electrons)
Metals vs non-metals — metals on the left/centre; non-metals on the right; metalloids on the staircase boundary
Transition metals — central block between groups 2 and 3; hard, dense, high melting points, coloured compounds

sections.title: History and Development
sections.text: The modern periodic table evolved through the work of several scientists, most notably Mendeleev, who arranged elements by properties and predicted missing elements.
points: Mendeleev (1869) — arranged elements by atomic mass AND similar properties; left gaps for undiscovered elements
Mendeleev's predictions — predicted properties of germanium ('eka-silicon') before its discovery; proved correct
Problem with Mendeleev — some elements out of order by mass but had correct properties (fixed by using atomic number)
Modern table — arranged by atomic NUMBER (protons), not mass; resolves anomalies in Mendeleev's version
Noble gases — discovered later and added as Group 0; fitted the pattern without disrupting it

sections.title: Trends Across Periods and Down Groups
sections.text: Properties change in predictable ways across periods and down groups, reflecting changes in electronic structure.
points: Across a period — atomic number increases, nuclear charge increases, metallic character decreases
Down a group — more electron shells, larger atomic radius, outer electrons further from nucleus
Reactivity (metals) — increases down a group (outer electron more easily lost)
Reactivity (non-metals) — decreases down a group (harder to gain electron into outer shell further away)
Melting points — generally higher for metals; trend varies across a period
Electronic configuration links — Na is 2,8,1 → Period 3, Group 1; Cl is 2,8,7 → Period 3, Group 7

keyTerms.def: A horizontal row in the periodic table — all elements have the same number of electron shells
A vertical column — elements with the same number of outer electrons and similar properties
Elements in the central block of the periodic table between groups 2 and 3
The number of protons in the nucleus; the basis for ordering the modern periodic table
The repeating pattern of properties seen across periods of the periodic table
Scientist who arranged elements by mass and properties in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements

examTips: Group 1 = 1 outer electron; Group 7 = 7 outer electrons; Group 0 = full outer shell — link group number to outer electrons.
Going down a group: same number of outer electrons, but more shells — explain reactivity trends using this.
Mendeleev ordered by atomic MASS; modern table orders by atomic NUMBER — examiners specifically ask about this distinction.
State the period number to give the number of electron shells (e.g. Period 3 elements have 3 shells).
commonMistakes: Confusing periods (horizontal rows) and groups (vertical columns) — periods go across the page.
Forgetting that Mendeleev used atomic MASS not atomic number — the modern table fixed anomalies by switching to atomic number.
Not explaining WHY reactivity changes down a group — always link to electron shell distance from nucleus.
clozePassages: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same vertical column are in the same group and have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer shell electrons. Elements in the same horizontal row are in the same period. The number of electron shells equals the period number. Metals are on the left and non-metals on the right.

Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table between groups 2 and 3. They have high melting points, are hard and dense, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. Many transition metals form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts. Iron, copper, and titanium are important transition metals used extensively in construction and engineering.

The properties of elements follow repeating patterns called periodicity. As you go across a period, elements change from metals to non-metals. Going down a group, elements become more reactive (for metals) or less reactive (for non-metals). The atomic radius increases down a group as more electron shells are added. These trends allow scientists to predict the properties of elements based on their position in the periodic table.

Groups.intro: Groups of elements share similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer electrons. Group 1, 7 and 0 are the most important for GCSE.
Groups.mnemonic: For Group 1 reactivity order: 'Little Sodium Keeps Rubbing Cesium Frantically' (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) — reactivity increases as you go down. For Group 7: 'Friendly Clumsy Brothers Ignore Arguments' (F, Cl, Br, I, At) — reactivity DECREASES going down.

sections.title: Group 1 — Alkali Metals
sections.text: Group 1 metals have 1 outer electron and react vigorously with water and air. Reactivity increases down the group.
points: 1 outer electron — easily lost to form M⁺ ion; highly reactive with water, air, and halogens
Reaction with water — metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen gas (e.g. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂)
Reactivity increases down group — outer electron is further from nucleus, less attraction, more easily lost
Reactivity order — Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs (lithium least reactive, caesium most)
Physical properties — soft, low density (Li, Na, K float on water), shiny when freshly cut
Storage — kept under oil to prevent reaction with oxygen and water in air

sections.title: Group 7 — Halogens
sections.text: Group 7 non-metals have 7 outer electrons and need 1 more to complete their shell. Reactivity decreases down the group.
points: 7 outer electrons — need to gain 1 electron to achieve full outer shell; form X⁻ ions
Reactivity decreases down group — outer shell is further from nucleus, electron harder to attract
Reactivity order — F > Cl > Br > I (fluorine most reactive, iodine least)
Displacement — more reactive halogen displaces less reactive from its salt solution (e.g. Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂)
Physical states at room temperature — F₂ and Cl₂ are gases; Br₂ is a liquid; I₂ is a solid
Colour — Cl₂ yellow-green; Br₂ red-brown; I₂ grey/violet vapour

sections.title: Group 0 — Noble Gases
sections.text: Noble gases have full outer electron shells, making them extremely unreactive. They exist as individual atoms.
points: Full outer shell — He has 2; Ne, Ar, Kr have 8 outer electrons; no tendency to gain or lose electrons
Monatomic — exist as single atoms, not molecules (unlike O₂, N₂ etc.)
Very unreactive (inert) — do not form compounds under normal conditions
Uses — helium in balloons/airships; neon in advertising signs; argon in light bulbs and welding (inert atmosphere)
Boiling point increases down group — larger atoms, stronger London dispersion forces between atoms
Density increases down group — heavier atoms

keyTerms.def: Group 1 elements — highly reactive metals with 1 outer electron; react with water to form hydroxide and hydrogen
Group 7 elements — reactive non-metals with 7 outer electrons; reactivity decreases down the group
Group 0 elements — unreactive monatomic gases with full outer shells
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt
Existing as molecules of two atoms (e.g. Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ — halogens exist as diatomic molecules)
Existing as single atoms — noble gases are monatomic
Chemically unreactive — used to describe noble gases due to their full outer shells

examTips: Group 1 reactivity INCREASES down the group — explain it: outer electron is further from nucleus, less nuclear attraction, more easily lost.
Group 7 reactivity DECREASES down the group — explain it: the outer shell is further away, so gaining an electron is harder.
Noble gases are inert because they have full outer electron shells — no need to gain or lose electrons.
For halogen displacement, state the colour change as evidence: e.g. colourless KBr solution turns orange/brown when Cl₂ is added (Br₂ formed).
commonMistakes: Saying Group 7 reactivity INCREASES down the group — it DECREASES (opposite to Group 1).
Forgetting that Group 1 metals are stored under oil — they react with both air (oxygen) and water.
Not explaining reactivity trends in terms of electron shell distance — always link to nuclear attraction and ease of gaining/losing electrons.
clozePassages: Group 1 elements are called alkali metals. They are very reactive metals that react vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. Lithium, sodium, and potassium are all stored in oil to prevent reaction with air or water.

Group 7 elements are called halogens. They are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules. Their reactivity decreases down the group. Fluorine is the most reactive, chlorine is a yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid. A more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt — this is called a displacement reaction.

Group 0 elements are called noble gases. They are extremely unreactive because their outer electron shells are full. They exist as individual atoms and do not form compounds under normal conditions. Helium is used in balloons and airships. Neon is used in advertising signs. Argon is used to provide an inert atmosphere in light bulbs and welding. Their low reactivity makes them very safe to use.

History of the Atom.intro: Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time as new experimental evidence emerged. This is a great example of how scientific models change.
History of the Atom.mnemonic: Remember the scientists in order with: 'Ducks Take Risks By Moonlight' — Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr, Modern model. Each scientist changed the model when new evidence emerged.

sections.title: Timeline of Atomic Models
sections.text: The model of the atom has been revised several times as new evidence emerged from experiments — a key example of how science progresses.
points: Dalton (1803) — solid spheres; atoms are indivisible; each element is a different sphere
Thomson (1904) — 'plum pudding' model; discovered electrons embedded in a positive sphere (like plums in pudding)
Rutherford (1909) — nuclear model from alpha scattering; most mass in a tiny, dense, positive nucleus; electrons around it
Bohr (1913) — electrons orbit in fixed circular shells at specific energy levels; refined Rutherford's model
Modern model — electrons in orbitals (probability clouds); nucleus contains protons and neutrons (Chadwick discovered neutron in 1932)
numbered: Thomson (1904) — 'plum pudding' model; electrons embedded in positive sphere
Rutherford (1909) — nuclear model; most mass in tiny positive nucleus; electrons around it (alpha scattering experiment)
Bohr (1913) — electrons in fixed circular orbits (shells) at specific energies
Modern model — electrons in orbitals (probability clouds); subatomic structure of nucleus

sections.title: Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment
sections.text: Rutherford's gold foil experiment was the key evidence that disproved the plum pudding model and established the nuclear model of the atom.
points: Setup — alpha particles (positive) fired at a very thin sheet of gold foil; detector surrounds the foil
Observation 1 — most alpha particles passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space)
Observation 2 — small number were deflected at large angles (hit the small positive nucleus)
Observation 3 — very few bounced straight back (nucleus is tiny, dense and positively charged)
Conclusion — the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus — disproves the plum pudding model
Why plum pudding was wrong — if positive charge were spread out (as Thomson said), no large deflections would occur

sections.title: How Models Change in Science
sections.text: The development of the atomic model shows how scientific knowledge evolves when new experimental evidence challenges existing models.
points: Evidence drives change — each new model replaced the old when experimental results could not be explained
Peer review — other scientists test and check new findings before they are accepted
Chadwick (1932) — discovered the neutron, completing the modern nuclear model
Bohr's improvement — Rutherford's model couldn't explain why electrons didn't spiral into nucleus; Bohr's fixed shells solved this
Modern quantum model — electrons exist in orbitals (regions of probability), not fixed circular orbits

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model with electrons embedded in a positive sphere — disproved by Rutherford
Rutherford's model with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus and electrons orbiting around it
Rutherford's experiment firing alpha particles at gold foil to probe atomic structure
A positively charged particle (2 protons, 2 neutrons) used in Rutherford's experiment
Model where electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells)
A neutral subatomic particle in the nucleus — discovered by Chadwick in 1932
A simplified representation of a system used to explain observations and make predictions

examTips: Describe Rutherford's results AND their meaning: most pass through = mostly empty space; some deflect = small positive nucleus; few bounce back = nucleus is tiny and very dense.
Models change when new evidence CANNOT be explained by the existing model — state this principle in 'How Science Works' questions.
Remember Thomson discovered the electron first (plum pudding); Rutherford then found the nucleus; Bohr added shells; Chadwick found the neutron.
In 6-mark questions, describe each scientist's model AND the evidence that led to its replacement.
commonMistakes: Saying Rutherford's experiment PROVED the plum pudding model — it DISproved it completely.
Forgetting that in the plum pudding model it was a POSITIVE sphere with electrons embedded — not a negative one.
Confusing who discovered what: Thomson = electron, Rutherford = nucleus, Bohr = shells, Chadwick = neutron.
clozePassages: Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. John Dalton proposed that atoms were solid, indivisible spheres. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model, where electrons were embedded in a positively charged sphere. Ernest Rutherford carried out the gold foil experiment and discovered the nucleus, replacing the plum pudding model.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, but some were deflected at large angles and a few bounced back. This showed the atom was mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre. Niels Bohr later refined the model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels called shells.

The modern model of the atom includes a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in orbitals at different energy levels. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, explaining why the mass of atoms was greater than the number of protons suggested. Scientific models are revised as new evidence emerges — the development of the atomic model is a good example of how science progresses through evidence and peer review.
